svg.text: Copying a tile of K into shared memory, line by line
A tile is a 64 × 64 block of K: 64 keys × 64 values. 128 threads, numbered 0 to 127, copy it together. They all run the same
lines, but each copies a different part. The figure follows one of them, thread 19, and draws its part in orange.
19 is just an example; every thread works the same way. Thread 0 would hide the arithmetic, since its numbers are all zero.

svg.text: # 64 // 8 = 8 threads per row of the tile
One row of K: D = 64 values
piece 0, zoomed in: 8 values × 2 bytes = 16 bytes = 128 bits
8 pieces per row, so 8 threads share each row: tpr = 8
dtype.width is the size of one value in bits. K is stored
in bf16, a number format that uses 16 bits (2 bytes) per
Why 128? It is the most one thread can move with a single
copy instruction: 128 bits, 16 bytes. Below, the 8 values
one thread copies at a time are called a piece.
D is the head dimension: the length of one row of K, 64
values. A row holds 64 // 8 = 8 pieces, so tpr = 8 threads
The atom: the one instruction that moves a piece

svg.text: CopyUniversalOp: a plain load into registers, then a plain store.
Each moves 128 bits = 16 bytes = one piece.
An atom is the one instruction a thread runs to move one
piece. make_copy_atom builds it from three choices:
CopyUniversalOp: the plain kind of copy. The thread loads
its piece from global memory into its registers, then
dtype: the values are bf16. num_bits_per_copy=128: one
instruction moves 128 bits, a whole piece.
Change only this line and the instruction changes, and
with it the speed. The next figure compares atoms.

svg.text: the 64 values of a row of K
self.threads is 128: the block's 4 warps (groups of 32
threads that run together) × 32. 128 // tpr = 16, so the
layout puts the threads in a grid of 16 rows × 8 columns.
stride=(tpr, 1) = (8, 1) numbers the spots. A stride is
how much the number grows per step in one direction: one
row down adds 8, one column right adds 1. So thread = 8 ×
row + column, and thread 19 sits at row 2, column 3.
Lay the grid over the top 16 rows of the tile: grid row r
copies row r of K, and column c copies piece c, values 8c

svg.text: one step: 16 × 8 threads, 1 piece each = 16 rows × 64 values
thread 19's piece in each step: values 24–31
make_layout((1, vec)) is the value layout: what each
thread copies per step, 1 row × 8 values. That is one
piece, exactly what one atom moves.
make_tiled_copy_tv (tv: thread and value) joins the atom
and the two layouts into g2s (global to shared): the plan
A step is one round in which every thread copies one
piece. One step covers 16 rows × 64 values, a quarter of
the tile. CuTe repeats the step 4 times, 16 rows lower
each time, so thread 19 copies values 24–31 of rows 2, 18,
Pick a thread: its share of the plan

So tKsK has the shape of tKgK without its last part.

svg.text: each step: load 16 bytes, store 16 bytes
All 128 threads at once: 128 × 4 pieces × 16 bytes = 8,192 bytes
tKgK[None, None, None, j] picks key block j. None keeps a
whole part of the shape, like : in NumPy, so only the last
cute.copy then runs the atom of step 2 once per piece: 4
times. Each time thread 19 loads 16 bytes from global
memory into its registers and stores them at the same row
The kernel runs this line once per key block: j = 0, 1, 2,
